summary: Mattel is facing criticism over its new Barbie honouring Wilma Mankiller, the first female Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, because of inaccuracies in the doll and packaging. Cherokee Nation Principal Chief Chuck Hoskin Jr said the basket isn't authentically Cherokee and the packaging's syllabary symbols read "Chicken Nation". Mattel did not work directly with the tribal government but says it is "discussing options", while Cherokee women voiced mixed emotions about the doll.
one_line: Mattel's Wilma Mankiller Barbie drew criticism from Cherokee leaders for an inauthentic basket and packaging text that reads "Chicken Nation".
key_facts: Mattel announced the Wilma Mankiller Barbie last month as part of its "Inspiring Women" series; the Cherokee Nation hosted a celebration event on 6 December.
Wilma Mankiller was the first female Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, leading the tribe for a decade until 1995, and died in 2010.
The doll wears a turquoise dress with ribbon striping representing the four directions and carries a basket, inspired by an iconic photo of Mankiller holding a woven basket.
Chuck Hoskin Jr, Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation, told The New York Times the doll's basket wasn't authentically Cherokee.
The wrong Cherokee syllabary symbols were used on the packaging, so the text reads "Chicken Nation" instead of Cherokee Nation.
Hoskin said he learned of the doll six months ago and that Mattel did not work directly with the Cherokee Nation, though Mattel later expressed some regret for not engaging them.
The Cherokee Nation said Mattel did not work with its design and communications team to secure or verify the official Seal.
Mattel spokesperson Devin Tucker said the company is aware of the syllabary problem and is "discussing options".
Mattel worked with Mankiller's estate, led by her husband Charlie Soap and her friend Kristina Kiehl.
Stacy Leeds, Arizona State University law school dean and former Cherokee Nation Supreme Court justice, described mixed emotions among Cherokee women who bought the doll.

Basket weaver Regina Thompson said the doll doesn't look like Mankiller, that traditional pucker toe moccasins should have replaced black shoes, and that "Wilma's name is the only thing Cherokee on that box."
Mankiller is the second Native American woman honoured with a Barbie, after aviator Bessie Coleman earlier this year; her likeness is also on a US quarter issued in 2021.
